strongest_angle: The 2026 Supreme Court decision in Chatrie v. United States establishes that police accessing Google Location History constitutes a Fourth Amendment search, affirming that individuals maintain a reasonable expectation of privacy in their cell-phone location data regardless of duration or third-party storage.

key_facts.fact: The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that police conducted a Fourth Amendment search when they acquired Okello Chatrie's location data from Google.

Justice Elena Kagan wrote that an individual has a reasonable expectation of privacy in records about his cell phone's location, even if the data was handed over by a third-party tech company for a limited time.
The ruling extends the logic of Carpenter v. United States, which held that accessing cell-site location information (CSLI) is a search because it provides an intimate window into a person's life.
The court rejected the government's argument that accessing only a short amount of location data does not count as a search, noting that even short-term monitoring can reveal sensitive associations.
The Court vacated the lower court's judgment and remanded the case to determine if the specific multi-step geofence warrant satisfied requirements of particularity and probable cause.
